source.title: A jamming transition from under- to over-parametrization affects generalization in deep learning
source.authors: Stefano Spigler; M. Geiger; Stéphane d'Ascoli; Levent Sagun; G. Biroli; M. Wyart

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; no apparent cut-off or corruption affecting the reported findings.
record.tranche_reason: The paper varies network size and measures training loss and unsatisfied training constraints to study when gradient-based fitting succeeds. It uses fully connected ReLU networks and a quadratic hinge loss, rather than the benchmark convolutional setups in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The study tests the size-versus-training-fit part of V1 and the depth-without-shortcuts part of V3, but on binary random-label and MNIST tasks using fully connected networks. It reports finite training runs and a numerically estimated jamming boundary. Values used to select or refine that boundary, including N* and NΔ/N plots, are extracted where text supplies the outcomes; figure-only curves are not transcribed as precise numbers.
record.test_reason: The study measures fitting and jamming in fully connected ReLU networks on binary random data and MNIST parity. V1 specifies convolutional networks on CIFAR-10/100; V3 specifies depth degradation in batch-normalized convolutional networks and its prevention by identity shortcuts. Neither is tested by these experiments. The study also does not test the teacher-student, initialization, stability-threshold, or normalization comparisons in the other versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors describe a jamming boundary separating positive training loss from attainable zero loss, and a generalization-error cusp near that boundary that disappears with early stopping. Their explanation for avoiding positive-loss minima is conditional on assumptions about effective parameter count and the loss Hessian; it is not an unconditional guarantee for arbitrary architectures or initializations.
record.recipe_differences: Fully connected ReLU networks trained primarily with hinge loss; binary random-label or MNIST parity tasks; size sweeps and finite-run transition estimation rather than the CIFAR convolutional benchmark recipes in the versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Training fit depends strongly on parameter count relative to dataset size (the jamming boundary); the estimated transition also varies with data structure and may depend on initialization, architecture, dynamics, and training time as discussed in the text. No plain-versus-shortcut comparison is reported.

fits_no_version.finding: Sufficiently wide fully connected ReLU networks reach zero hinge training loss on random binary data and MNIST parity; narrower networks cross a jamming boundary into positive loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For these fully connected binary-classification tasks and training protocols, increasing width permits gradient-based training to satisfy all training margins beyond an empirically estimated jamming boundary.

fits_no_version.finding: Varying depth, input dimension, and loss has little effect on the random-data fitting boundary, while MNIST requires significantly fewer parameters than random data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The fitting boundary in the tested fully connected networks depends strongly on data structure and comparatively weakly on the tested depth, input dimension, and loss choices.

fits_no_version.finding: MNIST parity test error has a cusp near jamming and declines with further width; selecting the minimum test error during training removes the cusp.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the tested fully connected MNIST parity networks, generalization depends nonmonotonically on width, with strong overfitting concentrated near the fitting transition.

record.peer_reviewed: Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and Theoretical
record.problems: The study focuses on binary tasks and fully connected networks, not the CIFAR convolutional benchmarks in V1. Training is finite; the authors discuss numerical precision issues and possible premature stopping for some near-transition runs. Transition locations and several curves are shown only in figures, without exact numerical values in the supplied text. There is no direct shortcut comparison.

untested.parts: Training classification error of convolutional networks on CIFAR-10/100, including random or corrupted labels and the specified training-recipe qualifications.
Spurious-minimum frequencies in two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems and the effect of one or two extra student neurons.
Depth degradation in plain batch-normalized convolutional networks, identity-shortcut comparisons, very deep plain tanh training, and Fixup residual training.
Initialization comparisons measuring training speed or trainable depth, including orthogonal versus Gaussian weights and orthogonal convolution kernels.
Learning rates relative to initial stability thresholds, transient loss and curvature dynamics, edge-of-stability training, and divergence.
Controlled normalization comparisons of training speed and learning-rate tolerance, including Fixup.

record.verdict_notes: The original V1 and V3 labels extend the versions beyond their specified systems. Near-transition failures in these experiments therefore do not limit those versions. Even for a broader fitting claim, positive hinge loss or positive NΔ alone would not demonstrate classification error, because correctly classified examples with insufficient margin also contribute. The source's inconsistent run counts require correction before quantitative aggregation.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, convolutional networks, Adam comparisons, corrupted-label benchmarks as distinct from random-label data, smaller-model/early-stopping/regularization comparisons.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems, spurious minima frequency, and student width relative to teacher width.

Batch-normalized convolutional networks, identity residual shortcuts, ImageNet, and CIFAR-10 comparisons; special initialization of very deep plain tanh networks; residual networks without normalization.
Activation-matched initialization comparisons, signal/gradient propagation outcomes, orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization comparisons, and 10,000-layer convolutional training.
Learning-rate stability threshold, loss-curvature dynamics, sharpness, and divergence outcomes.
Batch-normalization comparisons of training speed or learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup residual-network comparisons.

rows.operation_detail: Decreased width at fixed depth until training constraints remained unsatisfied; random inputs on a hypersphere with random labels.

conditions.value: 5·10^5 steps at learning rate 10^-2 then 5·10^5 at 10^-3; batch size min(P/2, 1024); batch normalization

rows.measure: Whether all training constraints are satisfied (NΔ=0) at the end of training; estimated transition N*.
rows.value: N* estimated by decreasing h until NΔ>0.1N; transition location plotted against P (figure only).
rows.locator: Appendix B.1, Details about Fig 3A hinge; Fig. 3A
rows.note: The paper describes a finite-run size sweep and its threshold criterion. The plot does not provide transcribable exact N* values in the supplied text.
rows.check: Fully connected random-data experiment falls outside V1. The conditions mix two protocols: Fig. 3A hinge uses orthogonal initialization, no batch normalization, and 2M full-batch Adam steps; default initialization, SGD, batch normalization, and 1M steps describe cross-entropy experiments. N* is an estimated transition location, not a partially observed classification-error result.

rows.measure: Fraction of unsatisfied training constraints NΔ/N across runs near transition.

starting at 10^-4; section 3 schedule divides by 10 every 250k steps

rows.measure: Count of runs by fraction NΔ/N of unsatisfied constraints.
rows.value: 37 runs had NΔ=0; 74 had NΔ>0.4N; 14 had NΔ between 1 and 4; 5 had 4<NΔ<0.4N.
rows.note: Authors attribute 14 runs to numerical precision issues and say they think the 5 remaining intermediate runs were stopped too early. These are near-transition outcomes, not a shortcut comparison.
rows.check: Outside V1 and V3; margin violations are not classification-error counts. The source itself is inconsistent: 37 + 74 + 14 + 5 equals 130, although it reports 128 runs. Preserve this discrepancy rather than computing rates. Outcomes also pool different P values across the transition and should not receive one partial-effect state.

rows.subject: fully-connected ReLU network (MNIST parity, L=5)
rows.operation_detail: Varied network width and measured final training loss behavior after finite training.
rows.measure: Training fit as width is increased beyond the estimated jamming point.
rows.value: The authors state that beyond the jamming point the model is in the over-parametrized phase where a global minimum is accessible; training loss is zero by the study's definition of that phase.
rows.note: Conclusion describes the over-parametrized phase generally; the size sweep is on MNIST at three P values.
rows.check: Duplicates R7 while presenting the general conclusion and definition of the over-parametrized phase as another experimental result. Remove as an independent result row. The experiment also falls outside V1.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Over-parametrized fully connected ReLU networks on the tested random-label and MNIST parity tasks
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports zero training loss above the jamming boundary and a size threshold separating fitting from positive training loss (R1, R2, R7, R8).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Finite-run fits near the jamming boundary, especially random data runs
reader_labels.reason: Several runs near transition retain many unsatisfied constraints; authors also flag intermediate outcomes as numerical-precision issues or possibly stopped too early (R3, R4, R5, R6).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Fully connected networks with depth L=2, 3, or 5 in this study
reader_labels.reason: Depth and training constraints are examined, but the results do not test whether plain convolutional networks degrade with depth or whether identity shortcuts prevent it (R3, R4, R5).
